column3: Digital Ceasefire and De-escalation Handbook Launched at the Paris Peace Forum
column5:
On 10 November 2026, the Human Rights Center at UC Berkeley School of Law officially launched the *Digital Ceasefire and De-escalation Handbook* at the [Paris Peace Forum](https://parispeaceforum.org/). The standing-room-only session, *Negotiating Peace in a Digital World*, brought participants together to explore how parties to conflict can negotiate agreements to constrain hostile digital operations, protect civilians, and advance peace.

![The audience facing the stage under the Paris Peace Forum sign, with the Eiffel Tower visible through the windows](assets/posts/paris-launch/photo-2.jpg)

The launch took place in a particularly significant setting: the Palais de Chaillot, where the United Nations General Assembly adopted the [Universal Declaration of Human Rights](https://www.ohchr.org/sites/default/files/UDHR/Documents/UDHR_Translations/eng.pdf) on 10 December 1948. Nearly eight decades later, the venue provided a fitting backdrop for a conversation about protecting human rights and advancing peace in an increasingly digitalized world.

![The three session speakers seated on stage, two of them holding copies of the Handbook, with the Eiffel Tower in fog behind them](assets/posts/paris-launch/photo-1.jpg)

Officially opened by [Francesca Bosco](https://unidir.org/people/francesca-bosco/), acting Head of the Security and Technology Programme at the United Nations Institute for Disarmament Research (UNIDIR), the launch was led by the Handbook’s co-authors, [Betsy Popken](https://humanrights.berkeley.edu/people/betsy-popken/) and [Brett Solomon](https://www.brettsolomon.info/), who introduced the Handbook and its accompanying interactive online platform before inviting participants to put its provisions into practice.

## Negotiating a Digital Ceasefire

Rather than following a traditional panel format, the session immersed participants in an interactive negotiation simulation. Working in pairs, participants assumed the roles of two opposing parties to an armed conflict in which a physical ceasefire was in place but remained fragile. Their challenge was to negotiate a digital ceasefire addressing internet shutdowns and throttling.

![Participants seated in rows wearing headphones and reading printed simulation materials](assets/posts/paris-launch/photo-3.jpg)

Drawing on the Handbook, participants were asked to negotiate three fundamental questions:

- What digital operations should be prohibited?
- What activities or limited exceptions should be permitted?
- What happens when something goes wrong?

The exercise exposed participants to some of the complexities of negotiating in the digital domain, including the private ownership of telecommunications infrastructure, military exceptions, humanitarian connectivity, attribution, and the role of third parties and proxies.

Midway through the simulation, participants were presented with an unfolding crisis: a major hospital had suddenly lost internet connectivity, one party accused the other of violating the ceasefire, and neither had conclusive evidence about who was responsible. Participants were challenged to revisit their agreements and consider whether the provisions they had negotiated were sufficient to respond to the crisis and prevent renewed hostilities.

![A full room of participants seen from the side of the stage during the session](assets/posts/paris-launch/photo-5.jpg)

The simulation generating lively negotiations across the room and demonstrating both the complexities and possibilities of negotiating digital ceasefires. The subsequent group discussion explored what makes such agreements difficult to negotiate, what provisions parties may initially overlook, and what mechanisms can help a digital ceasefire hold.

![The three speakers on stage during the discussion, one speaking into a microphone](assets/posts/paris-launch/photo-4.jpg)

## From Principles to Practice

The Handbook provides a practical framework for mediators, parties to conflict, and other stakeholders to negotiate digital ceasefires and de-escalation agreements in situations of armed conflict, grey zone activity, and other security contexts. It includes model provisions addressing internet interference, information threats, and cyber attacks, alongside provisions concerning technology companies, third parties, monitoring, and constructive digital operations.

Through the accompanying online platform, users can select, adapt, and [build their own agreements](https://digitalceasefirehandbook.org/#/builder) to reflect the circumstances in which they are negotiating.

The Paris Peace Forum launch marks the beginning of the next phase of the initiative: supporting mediators and parties engaged in negotiations, conducting workshops and trainings with conflict-affected communities, and advancing the international conversation on constraining digital hostilities.

As warfare becomes increasingly digitalized, the processes through which we negotiate, maintain, and build peace must evolve with it.
